Ἑβραῖοι ἐπέγραψαν τὴν βίβλον Σέφρα ϑελείμ. ἐν δὲ ταῖς πράξεσι τῶν ἀποστόλων ,«βίθλος ψαλμῶν“ εἶναι λέγεται. ἔχει δὲ ἢ λέξις οὕτως ,,ος γέγραπται ἐν βίβλῳ ψαλμῶν. ὄνομα δὲ ἐν τῇ ἐπιγραφῇ τοῦ βιβλίου οὐ κεῖται ἐνταῦϑα, ἡ δὲ αἰτία τὸ μὴ ἑνὸς λόγους ἀναγεγράφϑαι ἐπὶ τοῦτο, ἀλλὰ πλειόνων συνειλέχϑαι. τοῦ Ἔσδρα. ὡς αὖ παραδόσεις φασίν, μετὰ τὴν αἰχμαλωσίαν συναγαγόντος ψαλμοὺς πλειόνων εἰς ἕν ἢ καὶ λόγους οὐ πάντως ὄντας ψαλμούς. προτέταχται γοῦν ἐπὶ μὲν τινῶν τὸ Δαυΐδ ὄνομα, ἐπὶ δὲ ἑτέρων τὸ Σολομῶν καὶ ἐπὶ ἄλλων τοῦ σάφ. εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ τοῦ Ἰδιϑούμ τινες καὶ παρὰ τούτους ἄλλοι τῶν υἱῶν Κορέ, ὡς καὶ δΜΙωσέως. τῶν οὖν τοσούτον ἐπὶ 1ὅ τὸ αὐτὸ συναχϑέντες οἱ λόγοι οὐκ ἂν ὑπὸ τοῦ εἰδότος λέγοιντο μόνου τοῦ Δαυΐδ. ζητητέον δὲ περὶ τῶν ἀνεπιγράφων, τίνος αὐτοὺς χρὴ ὑπονοεῖν. διὰ τί γὰρ κἂν ἡ ἁπλουστάτη ἐπιγραφὴ οὐ πρόκειται αὐτῶν, ἥτις οὕτως ἔχει͵, , Τοῦ Δαυὶδ ψαλμὸς“ ἢ ,,ἸΤἸοῦ Δαυϊδ΄'΄ χωρὶς πάσης προσϑήκης; ὑπενοήσαμεν δέ. ὅπου αὕτη μόνη ἐπιγραφὴ ἐστιν, ὅτι οὔτε ψαλμός ἐστι τὸ λεγόμενον οὔτε ὠδή. ἀλλὰ λόγος τις ἐξ ἁγίου πνεύμεῖτος ὠφελείας ἕνεκεν τῆς τοῦ δυναμένου συνιέναι ἀναγεγραμμένος. pass_a_gloss: The book of Psalms contains new teaching, after the legislation of Joshua, and when the second book after the writing of Joshua, a didactic book is found. After the death of Moses and Joshua, David, who became like a savior, being deemed worthy as a father, first handed over a new way of psalmody to the Hebrews, through which he abolishes the things legislated by Moses concerning sacrifices, and introduces a new way of worship of God through hymns and shouts, and teaches many other things that surpass the law of Joshua in the matter of his work. And this is the purpose and usefulness of the book. The reason for the title is that most of the Gentiles who have believed in Christ think that this book belongs to David. And they entitle it Psalms of David, we must say what has come to us about it. The Hebrews entitled the book Sepher Tehilim. And in the Acts of the Apostles, it is said to be the book of Psalms. And the phrase is found thus, as it is written in the book of Psalms. But the name is not found in the title of the book, and the reason is that not one person's words are written, but many are gathered together. According to tradition, Ezra, after the captivity, gathered psalms of many into one, and also words that are not necessarily psalms. For on some, the name of David is written, on others the name of Solomon, and on others something else. And there are some of Jeduthun and others of the sons of Korah, as well as those of Moses. Therefore, the words gathered in this way would not be said to be only of David. But we must investigate the untitled ones, whose they should be thought to be. For why is even the simplest title not placed before them, which is thus, Of David a psalm, or Of David? We have thought that where this alone is the title, the thing said is not a psalm or a song, but a word from the Holy Spirit, written for the benefit of the one who can understand. A tradition of a Hebrew came to me about the last ones. Since many were untitled, and one before these untitled ones has the title Of David, he said that those also should be thought to be of David, taken in common. And if this is so, it follows that the untitled ones are of those whose predecessors are well thought to be according to the title. The prophet entitled the present book of Psalms a psaltery. For, they say, only on musical instruments is the active bronze brought from above, not from below like the others, so that those who have learned it may keep the analogy of such a name and look to the things above, from which it was sounded, for this reason he entitled it a psaltery. For it is an echo and sound of the all-holy Spirit.

pass_b_english: The Book of Psalms contains a new teaching, coming after the legislation of Joshua; indeed, it is the second instructional book to appear after Joshua's writing. After the deaths of Moses and Joshua, David — becoming a kind of savior, deemed worthy as a father — was the first to hand down a new way of psalmody to the Hebrews. Through it he abolished the sacrificial regulations legislated by Moses and introduced a new way of worshiping God through hymns and shouts, while also teaching many other things that go beyond Joshua's law in the matter of his work. That is the purpose and usefulness of this book. The reason for its title is this: most Gentiles who have believed in Christ think this book belongs to David, and so they call it the Psalms of David; therefore we must tell what has come down to us concerning it. The Hebrews entitled the book Sepher Tehillim, and in the Acts of the Apostles it is called the Book of Psalms (Acts 1:20). The phrasing appears as "as it is written in the Book of Psalms." Yet no author's name stands in the title of the book itself, and the reason is that the words gathered here are not from one person but from many. According to tradition, Ezra, after the captivity, collected psalms of many authors into one volume, along with words that are not necessarily psalms. On some the name of David is prefixed, on others the name of Solomon, on others something else; there are also some of Jeduthun and others of the sons of Korah, as well as those of Moses. Therefore the words gathered in this way could not be said to belong to David alone. We must inquire about the untitled ones — whose they should be thought to be. For why is even the simplest title not placed before them, a title such as "A Psalm of David" or simply "Of David"? We have reasoned that where this alone is the title, the piece is neither a psalm nor a song, but a word from the Holy Spirit, written for the benefit of the one who can understand. A tradition from a certain Hebrew came to me about the last psalms. Since many were untitled, but the one immediately preceding these untitled ones bears the title "Of David," he said that those also should be regarded as David's, taken in common; and if that is so, it follows that the untitled ones belong to those whose preceding titles are well established. The prophet named the present book of Psalms a Psaltery. For, they say, only on musical instruments is the active bronze sounded from above, not from below like the others, so that those who have learned it may preserve the analogy of such a name and look upward, to the source from which it resounded; for this reason he called it a Psaltery. For it is the echo and sound of the all-holy Spirit. — Origen on the Psalms.
